rows: 24 ga. single wall or listed double wall

steps: Site & clearances

Never in a sleeping room. Hold the stove (B, D, F) and pipe (A, C, E) minimums from p. 9; pipe clearances are to the pipe's outside diameter. Alcoves need double-wall pipe and 56" wide × 84" tall minimum.

Pick a central spot in the main living area; an uninsulated basement or a garage is an inefficient location. Maintain the structural integrity of floor, walls and ceiling/roof; add bracing if required and never cut a load-bearing wall or engineered truss. Clearances may be reduced only by methods in NFPA 211.
Floor protection
Non-combustible Type 1 (ember) protection under the stove: 6" to the sides (G, to the top plate) and 16" in front (H, to the face). Through-wall: 2" either side of the horizontal connector.
Assemble the stove
Uncrate; each piece is boxed with its own instructions. It's heavy — get a second person. Assemble in the manual's order, legs or pedestal before standing it up.

1. Lay the stove on to its back
  2. Install the Ash Pan Kit (optional)
  3. Install the Legs or Pedestal Kit
  4. Carefully set the stove upright
  5. Install the catalyst and flame diffuser
  6. Install the door
  7. Install the blower (optional)
Don't use the stove without the baffle boards and ceramic insulation packaged with it.
Chimney & connector
Min. 6" listed UL 103HT chimney or NFPA 211 lined masonry. Connector: 24 ga. single-wall black or listed double wall; 3 screws per joint, including 3 at the stove.

Double wall is recommended for better draft and less creosote. Single-wall pipe only as a connector to an approved masonry or stainless steel chimney — never as the chimney or through a wall or ceiling. Don't connect to a flue serving another appliance or to any air distribution or duct system. Depending on the double-wall pipe, it may also need fastening at the chimney (p. 4).
Roof exit & flue height
Exit the roof by 3 feet minimum and 2 feet above any roof within 10 feet. Recommended flue height runs from 14 ft (no offsets) to 22 ft (90° offsets into an exterior chimney).
All-fuel chimney
Follow the chimney maker's manual; UL-103HT, one brand only, no damaged parts. No connector through an attic, closet, wall, floor or ceiling; insulation shield in attics.

Examples named: DuraTech (DuraVent), Ultra Temp (Selkirk), Excel (ICC Chimney), Temp/Guard (Metal-Fab). Many systems need a 2" air space around the pipe. Install supports, braces, shielding and firestops per the chimney manufacturer. On snowy metal roofs, consider snow breaks or diverters.
Mobile home extras
Outside air kit KA OA 1 and listed double-wall connector are required. Ground the stove to the home's metal frame with 8-gauge wire through the hearth; fasten to the floor where code requires.
Masonry chimney
Have it cleaned and inspected first. Install a UL 1777 type HT (2100°) liner no smaller than 6" or 28 square inches; combustible-wall pass-throughs per NFPA 211.

Kuma recommends an insulated liner for performance and easier cleaning; any reduction in flue size may cause smoking or poor performance. A damaged or non-compliant chimney may need re-lining or rebuilding. The wall pass-through method is reprinted from NFPA 211-2016 as a figure on p. 16 and isn't transcribed here.
Break-in fire
Brief the owner: start small and raise the heat slowly over 4 to 5 hours to cure the paint. Ventilate — the smell and haze are normal and fade.

panels.title: Smoke into the room
items: Bypass rod not pulled open → open it, and open the bypass 1 minute before the door
Door opened too quickly → crack it and let the stove breathe a few seconds
Cold chimney, reverse draft → open a door or window about 5 minutes, restart with newspaper strips and kindling
Dirty chimney or cap → clean it; screened caps can block in a few weeks

panels.title: Lazy or won't burn hot
items: Chimney still cool → allow more time to warm up
Green or wet wood → season about 1 year; cover the top, leave sides open
Shut down too soon → leave the air open longer
Catalyst plugged with ash → clean in place with ~20-30 psi air
Barometric episodes → usually pass within a few days

panels.title: Won't shut down · short burns
items: Door or glass gasket not sealing → check the gaskets
Chimney too tall → see flue height recommendations
Load too small or wood too large for the coal bed → rekindle first

panels.title: Catalyst faults
items: Plugged with creosote (wet wood, bypass rod pushed in too soon) → burn a hot fire, brush the face
Masked with soot or fly ash (bypass pushed in too soon; cardboard, coal, wrapping paper) → remove flame guard, brush or blow out
Lower efficiency (flames on the catalyst from excess draft) → less wood, less air, or a damper

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Two controls on the right side do the work: the air control (lower right) and the bypass control (upper right).

  1. Open the air. Slide the air control out, away from the stove, until it stops.
  2. Open the bypass. Pull it toward you about ¾" and down. Heat goes straight up the chimney, warming it quickly and keeping smoke out of the room while the door is open.
  3. Build the fire right on the fire brick, with no grate. For a "top down" fire, put larger pieces on the bottom, smaller pieces above and kindling on top, with a fire starter such as shredded paper on the kindling. Only small twigs and branches go in unsplit.
  4. Light it. You can leave the door slightly cracked to help it start. Close the door once the fire is well lit.
  5. Close the bypass after 15 minutes, or once the catalytic thermometer enters the active range. Lift the control and you'll feel it return to the closed position.
  6. Leave the air open for 20-30 minutes, then slide the air control in to set your burn rate. Shut it down too soon and the fire may go out or the catalyst may stop working.
Note: p. 19 says to leave the air control open for 20-30 minutes once the bypass is closed; p. 23 says to set it to high for 20 to 30 minutes when starting; the tips on p. 20 say to burn at high for 10-30 minutes when you start the stove, and to keep a medium to high firing rate for about 20 minutes when starting a cold stove.
Never use gasoline, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire. Don't leave the stove unattended with the door open. Do not over-fire the stove: trying to get more heat than it's designed for can permanently damage the stove and the catalyst.

heat.title: Setting the heat
heat.html:
The air control on the lower right sets the burn rate: slide it out for more heat, in for less. Any position in between works too.

Fully closed · low burn10-12 hours
About ¼" open · medium burn6-8 hours
Fully open · start-up or high2-3 hours

Burn times are approximate. Never over-fire the stove by leaving the air control on high for too long.

Read the catalytic thermometer

  • In the active range (anywhere in the light grey area): normal. Stay here.
  • Above the active range: you're past the catalyst's recommended operating temperature (1300°F). Short periods are fine, but if the probe is climbing, slide the air control in so that you do not over-fire the stove or the catalyst.
  • Below the active range: the stove is getting too cool to run efficiently. Reload before the catalyst goes inactive.
The stove has a factory-set minimum low burn rate. Don't alter it; that's against federal regulations.

reload.title: Adding more wood
reload.html:
1. Slide the air control fully open and pull the bypass open, just as when you light a fire. Wait 5 minutes so the coals become active and the smoke drafts up the chimney.
  2. Open the loading door slowly: crack it a little and let the stove breathe a few seconds first. Rake the coals, breaking up larger pieces, add wood and shut the door.
  3. Once the catalytic thermometer is in the active range and the new wood is well lit, close the bypass.
  4. Leave the air control open until the fire is well established, then set your burn rate. This matters most when rekindling a cool fire or one that has burned down to charcoal.
Note: the manual gives different times for leaving the air open after reloading: 10-20 minutes in the reloading steps (p. 20), both 20-30 and 10-30 minutes in the tips on the same page, and 20 to 30 minutes on p. 23 and p. 26.

Shutting the air down too early can cause excess creosote in the chimney; small, hot fires make less creosote than long, low, smoldering ones. Put large pieces only on a very hot, active bed of coals.

firstfire.title: Your first fires
firstfire.html:
Break it in slowly

The paint cures with heat, and that needs to happen slowly. For your first fire, start small and raise the heat gradually over 4 to 5 hours.

A smell or a haze

As the paint cures it gives off a smell, sometimes with a visible haze in the room. Keep the area well ventilated. The smell fades after a few hours of burning.

Popping and creaking

The metal moves as it heats up and cools down. That popping or creaking is normal and will likely ease after the first several weeks.

Lazy first fires

The first few fires often seem a bit lazy. As moisture evaporates from the brick, the fire gets more active. A layer of ash on the bottom helps keep the coal bed hot, and a good thick coal bed with a full load of wood gives the best performance.

The stove's surface color changes naturally as it's fired. That's considered normal.

wood.title: Choosing wood
wood.html:
Moisture in the wood is the leading cause of creosote buildup in the stove and chimney. Burn natural wood only.

Seasoning1 full year, protected from rain
Moisture content20% or less (use a moisture meter)
Recommended length18"

Air-dried, seasoned hardwoods generally give higher efficiency and lower emissions than softwoods or green, freshly cut hardwoods, and harder, denser woods burn longer. Cover the top of your woodpile but leave the sides open so air keeps drying it.

Never burn

  • Garbage, lawn clippings or yard waste
  • Anything containing rubber (including tires), plastic or asbestos
  • Waste petroleum products, paints, paint thinners or asphalt products
  • Construction or demolition debris, railroad ties or pressure-treated wood
  • Manure, animal remains, or salt-water driftwood and other salt-soaked materials
  • Unseasoned wood, paper products, cardboard, plywood or particleboard

Burning any of these may release toxic fumes, or make the stove ineffective and cause smoke.

Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine. Coal and wrapping paper can mask the catalyst; colored paper, paneling, and painted or treated wood can poison it.

ashes.title: Emptying the ashes
ashes.html:
Empty the ashes when they're 3" to 4" deep. Make sure the fire is out first; emptying ashes from an active or full fire will overheat the stove. Always wear gloves.

Scoop them out through the loading door, or use the ash drawer if your stove has one:

  1. Turn the ash drawer handle left or right to release the latch.
  2. Pull out the drawer and empty it.
  3. Clean out any ash that fell into the cavity the drawer slides into. Leftover ash can stop the pan sealing and let too much air reach the fire.
  4. Slide the drawer back in, push to compress the spring and turn the handle down.
Never run the stove with the ash drawer removed or open.
  • Leave 1" of ash in the stove; it helps keep a hot charcoal bed.
  • Dump ashes into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid and keep it away from the house.
  • Never use a combustible container such as a plastic bucket or paper bag, and never leave ashes near the house or garage.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
Your stove has an air wash that keeps the glass clean on its own. Help it by burning on high for 20 to 30 minutes every time you add wood. If smoke deposits build up from slow burning, set the air control to high for 20 to 30 minutes.

If it still needs cleaning

  • Never clean the glass while it's hot.
  • Use a soft cloth and stove glass cleaner.
  • No steel wool, sandpaper or abrasive cleaners.
Watch your wood length. Closing the door on a piece that's too long will break the glass. If the glass breaks, shut off the air control, let the fire burn out and don't leave the stove unattended. Don't use it again with broken glass.

Kuma replacement glass comes with the gasket pre-installed; parts are available from your dealer or kumastoves.com. Glass shattered by wood impact isn't covered by the warranty.

care.title: Chimney & yearly care
care.html:
Chimney & connectorat least once every two months in the heating season
Catalyst (visual check)at least three times a heating season
Door, glass & ash pan gasketsat least once a year
Bricks & ceramic insulationannually
Note: p. 25 says to inspect the chimney connector and chimney at least once every two months during the heating season; the troubleshooting pages (pp. 30-31) say your chimney should be checked and cleaned, if necessary, every few months.
  • Chimney: slow fires leave creosote in the flue, and it burns extremely hot if it ignites. Remove any buildup; Kuma recommends a licensed, professional chimney sweep. A damaged chimney must be replaced.
  • Gaskets: look for frayed or missing spots and press with a finger; they should feel somewhat soft. Hard gaskets leak air. If the cold glass moves, tighten the retaining-ring screws or replace the gasket.
  • Catalyst: pull the flame deflector forward to see it. If it isn't falling apart, crushed or excessively warped, it's likely fine. Clean ash off in place with a soft brush or ~20-30 psi of air.
  • Bricks: cracked bricks are fine if they stay in place; crumbling ones need replacing.
  • Ceramic insulation: it sits on top of the baffle. To replace it, remove the 4 burn tubes so the whole baffle comes down and out, noting their order so each goes back in the same place.
The manual also prints "remove the 3 burn tubes" here (p. 27); the same paragraph says to re-install "the 4 burn tubes", and the parts list (p. 29) names front, middle front or middle rear, and rear tubes.

safety.title: Safety & over-firing
safety.html:
Do not over-fire the stove. If any part of the stove or chimney glows, it's over-firing. Shut the air control off immediately. Trying to get more heat than the stove is designed for can permanently damage the stove and the catalyst.
  • The stove is hot while it's running. Keep children, clothing and furniture away; contact can burn skin.
  • A stove that isn't drafting properly can let smoke and carbon monoxide into the home. Smoke detectors and carbon monoxide monitors are recommended in the same room.
  • Never use gasoline, engine oil, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids, and keep them well away from the stove.
  • Keep the door closed while burning; crack it open only during start-up.
  • Don't use the stove with broken glass, and don't slam the door or strike the glass.
  • Never install it in a sleeping room.
  • Keep a type A:B:C fire extinguisher, checked regularly, where everyone knows to find it. NFPA recommends one on each floor.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Kuma's limited warranty covers the original owner from the date of purchase, for stoves bought from an authorized Kuma dealer. It isn't transferable.

Bricks, gasket, ceramic insulation, paint3 years parts · no labor
Blowers, brick supports, removable wear items5 years parts · 3 years labor
Firebox, burn tubes, legs, glass (thermal breakage), door castingForever parts · 3 years labor

Catalyst: a 6-year structural warranty (return it to Kuma; replaced free if it fails from a manufacturing defect) and a 12-year performance warranty (one replacement at a 50% discount from MSRP).

Register within 30 days at kumastoves.com, or return the registration in your owner's packet.

Not covered (examples)

  • Surface color changes, firebox noise from expansion, discolored plating or glass
  • Glass shattered by wood impact
  • Wrong fuel or accelerants, unauthorized changes, or ignoring the installation instructions or local codes
  • Abuse, over-firing, unauthorized repair, improper installation or service

specOutput.title: Output, efficiency & emissions
specOutput.html:
Heat output (test)11,219 to 30,612 Btu/hr
Maker's website: Cordwood BTU's 82,000 (30,612 EPA est.).
Efficiency77.8% (High Heating Value)
Maker's website: Efficiency (HHV) 78%.
Maker's website: Efficiency (LHV) 84%.
Particulate1.11 grams per hour
CO (average)0.49 grams per minute

Model K-251, catalyst equipped: secondary burn tubes plus an Applied Catalysts ACI-5M combustor. Meets the 2020 U.S. EPA crib wood emission limits for wood heaters sold after May 15, 2020; rates are under specific test conditions. Emissions tested to ASTM E2515 and ASTM E2780 (report 0123WM014E), safety tested to UL 1482-2022 (report 0123WS012S); tested and listed by OMNI-Test Laboratories.

The manufacturer-set minimum low burn rate must not be altered, and the stove must not be run with the catalytic element deactivated or removed.

specFuel.title: Fuel & burn rates
specFuel.html:
Recommended wood length18"
Moisture content20% or less
Seasoning1 full year

Natural wood only, built directly on the fire brick (no grate). Burn-rate table, p. 19:

Low · fully closed10-12 hours
Maker's website: Burn Time 12 hours.
Medium · about ¼" open6-8 hours
Start-up / high · fully open2-3 hours

Catalytic activity needs 500° to 700°F; a working combustor typically holds above 500°F and often exceeds 1,000°F. A probe reading above the active range means above the catalyst's recommended operating temperature (1300°F).

specChimney.title: Chimney & connector
specChimney.html:
Chimneylisted UL 103HT factory-built, min. 6" diameter
MasonryNFPA 211, with UL 1777 liner (type HT, 2100°)
Liner sizenot smaller than 6" or 28 square inches
Connector24 ga. single-wall black or listed double wall
Roof exit3 feet min.; 2 feet above roof within 10 feet
Stove top to capat least 14 feet
  • 3 screws per pipe joint, including 3 securing the pipe to the stove; some double-wall pipe also needs fastening at the chimney (p. 4).
  • Single-wall pipe only as a connector to an approved masonry or stainless steel chimney; never as a chimney, through a wall or ceiling, or in a mobile home.
  • Kuma recommends double wall for improved draft and less creosote.
  • Don't connect to a flue serving another appliance or to any air distribution or duct system.

specFlue.title: Flue height recommendations
specFlue.html:
No offsets in the chimney14 ft
30° or 45° offsets15 ft
90° offsets16 ft
90° offsets with 2-3 feet of horizontal run20 ft
90° offsets into exterior chimney22 ft

Recommended for proper draft. A chimney that is too short reduces draft (back-puffing, creosote, smoke and carbon monoxide leaking at appliance and connector joints); one that is too tall increases it, and "stove won't shut down" is one symptom. Cold, dense or moist air, obstructions, wind blowing down the chimney and creosote buildup also reduce draft.

specClear.title: Clearances to combustibles
specClear.html:
Minimums with single-wall / double-wall connector. The drawing on p. 9 shows where each letter is measured; the text doesn't name the walls.

A (pipe)15" / 10"
B (stove)11.5" / 7"
C (pipe)24.5" / 23.5"
D (stove)14.5" / 14"
E (pipe)15" / 14.5"
F (stove)5" / 5"
L18.5" / 18.5"
N84" / 84"
Alcove (double-wall pipe only)56" wide min. · 84" tall min.

Pipe clearances (A, C, E) are to the pipe's outside diameter, which varies by brand; both stove and pipe clearances must meet the minimums. The drawing also carries the note "18" or follow pipe manufacturer's instructions." Reduce clearances only by approved methods in NFPA 211, and follow local codes.

specFloor.title: Floor protection
specFloor.html:
G · sides (to the top plate)6"
H · front (to the stove face)16"
TypeType 1 (ember protection)
InsulationNo R-value required

Non-combustible, underneath the stove and extending to the sides and front. Through-wall installations: the hearth must extend underneath and 2" to either side of the horizontal connector pipe. In a mobile home the ground wire is run through the hearth to the frame.

specMobile.title: Manufactured (mobile) homes
specMobile.html:
• Outside air kit KA OA 1 is required for all mobile home installations; follow the instructions in its box.
  • Listed double-wall connector pipe is required; single wall may not be used as a connector.
  • Using 8-gauge ground wire and appropriate connectors, drill through the hearth and connect the stove to the metal frame underneath the home.
  • Fasten the stove to the floor when local code requires it.
  • Maintain the structural integrity of the floor, wall and ceiling/roof. Not in a sleeping room.

conflicts.issue: How long to leave the air control open / on high after reloading: 10-20 minutes (reloading step 4, p. 20) vs 20-30 minutes and 10-30 minutes (tips, p. 20) vs 20 to 30 minutes (p. 23 and p. 26). Start-up: leave the air control open 20-30 minutes once the bypass is closed (p. 19) and set it to high for 20 to 30 minutes (p. 23), but the p. 20 tips say high burn for 10-30 minutes and a medium to high firing rate for about 20 minutes for a cold stove.
Ceramic insulation replacement says remove 'the 3 burn tubes' and then re-install 'the 4 burn tubes' (p. 27); the parts list (p. 29) lists front, middle front or middle rear, and rear burn tubes.

Chimney inspection interval: the chimney connector and chimney should be inspected 'at least once every two months during the heating season' (p. 25) vs 'Your chimney should be checked and cleaned, if necessary, every few months' (troubleshooting, p. 30 twice and p. 31).

review.notes: The manual covers Ashwood LE-1, Wood Classic LE-1 and Cambridge LE-1 together as Model K-251 and distinguishes them only by per-model dimensional drawings (Wood Classic p. 6, Ashwood p. 7, Cambridge p. 8). Those pages, the certification tag (p. 5), the intake-air section (p. 12, heading only), the typical all-fuel installation (p. 14), the NFPA 211 wall pass-through figure (p. 16), the maintenance diagram (p. 28) and the thermometer/cut-away illustrations are figures with no extractable text; nothing was transcribed from them. Every number in the text (output, emissions, clearances, floor protection, chimney, flue heights) is common to all three models, so no per-model value rows were possible; the Dimensions card points to each model's drawing page instead. Clearance letters A-F, L, N (p. 9): the text gives the values and says A/C/E are pipe and B/D/F stove clearances, but which wall each letter is measured from (and what L, N and the note '18” or follow pipe manufacturer’s instructions' refer to) is only in the drawing; the guide shows letters only. The catalog's wall mapping for A-F could not be verified from the text. Catalog values the manual text does not state (not checked): 82,000 BTU/hr cordwood output, 2,800 sq ft heating area, 2.5 cu ft firebox, height/width/depth, weights, 125 cfm blower; the catalog's 30,612 BTU/hr, 1.11 g/hr, 18 in wood, 6 in flue, 12-hour burn and clearance values match pp. 3, 9, 11, 17, 19. Chimney inspection 'at least once every two months during the heating season' (p. 25) vs 'checked and cleaned, if necessary, every few months' (troubleshooting, pp. 30-31) is shown as a note in the care drawer and recorded in conflicts (spot-check, Oct 12). Minor wording differences not shown as conflicts: the 1/4-inch buildup example cites an 8” chimney (pp. 30, 31) and a 6” chimney (p. 30), not used in the guide; the part at the face of the baffle is called flame diffuser (p. 11), flame deflector and flame guard (p. 26) and catalytic flame guard KR-FG-01 (p. 29). Burn and time ranges are written with hyphens as printed (e.g. 20-30 minutes). No French or scrambled text in this manual.
